problemText: Read this sentence from a story: 'The dog barked loudly when the mailman arrived at the gate.' Which part of this sentence is an EXPLICIT statement?
choices: The mailman felt scared by the dog's reaction because we must infer the mailman's emotions from context clues in the story.
The dog was protective of its owner's house based on what we can understand about the dog's behavior and purpose.
The dog barked loudly when the mailman arrived at the gate.
The dog had been trained to guard the property as shown by details we can figure out from the text.
hints: An explicit statement uses plain words that are written right there in the text.
Look for a fact you can point to word for word, with nothing to figure out.

problemText: Read this passage: 'Yuki had studied the spelling list every night for a week. On test day, she wrote each word carefully and checked her work twice before turning in her paper.' Which statement is an INFERENCE, not something the text states directly?
choices: Yuki studied the spelling list every night for a week.
The spelling test happened on a day Yuki had prepared for.
She checked her work twice before turning in her paper.
Yuki wanted to do well on the spelling test.
hints: An inference is something the text does not say in plain words but that you figure out from the details.
Look for a statement about what Yuki was thinking or feeling, not just what she did.

problemText:
A student read this passage and made the claim below. Is this claim an inference supported by textual evidence, or is it just restating something the text already says explicitly?

Passage: 'Kai arrived at soccer practice with his shin guards already on and his cleats laced tight.'

Student's claim: 'Kai arrived at soccer practice ready to play right away.'

Which is true?
choices: It is a valid inference because no sentence in the passage says Kai was ready to play.
It is just a restatement because the passage already says Kai had his shin guards on and cleats laced.
It is a guess because the passage does not explain why Kai wore his gear.
It is an assumption because being ready to play requires knowledge about soccer that the passage does not teach.
hints: Check whether any sentence in the passage uses the exact words 'ready to play.'
An inference combines details the text gives to reach a new conclusion; a restatement just rewrites what was already said.

problemText:
Read this passage, then decide which statement is a valid inference with proper textual evidence.

Passage: 'The library's new computer lab had been closed for three weeks. When it finally opened on Monday, there was a line of twenty students waiting at the door before the librarian unlocked it. By Wednesday, the computers were all taken up during lunch period, and a sign-up sheet had to be posted.'

Which inference below is best supported by evidence from the text?
choices: Students are not interested in using computers at school because they did not sign up for the scheduled time slots.
Students had been waiting to use the new computer lab and wanted to access it as soon as it became available.
The library ordered new computers because the old ones were broken and could no longer support student use.
The librarian decided to close the lab because too many students were using it at once and needed to manage access.
hints: Look for details showing student behavior and what those details suggest about student interest.
Point to the exact phrases that prove your answer: what did students do when the lab opened, and what does that tell you about how much they wanted it?

problemText:
A student read this passage and wrote an inference. Read both, then decide if the inference needs to be fixed because it includes information from outside the text.

Passage: 'Every afternoon at three o'clock, Mr. Chen locked his classroom door and walked to the gymnasium. He always carried a stack of clipboards and a whistle. The gymnasium was where students gathered for practice after school.'

Student's inference: 'Mr. Chen coaches a school sports team because he is athletic and loves to exercise.'

What should the student do to fix this inference?
choices: Change 'coaches' to 'works with' because the passage does not use the word coaches to describe Mr. Chen's role.
Remove the phrase 'a school sports team' because the passage never mentions a specific sport or team name.
Remove the phrase 'because he is athletic and loves to exercise' because those ideas come from outside the passage, not from its details.
Keep the entire inference but add supporting details about Mr. Chen's personality traits because the clipboard and whistle prove he must be someone who enjoys physical activity and fitness.
hints: An inference can only use details the passage itself provides; 'athletic' and 'loves to exercise' are not mentioned in the text.
Check whether the text actually says anything about why Mr. Chen does what he does, or whether the student added an outside belief.

problemText:
Read this passage, then answer the question that follows.

Passage: 'Jamila skipped her usual route through the park and took the long street instead. When she passed the old community center, she slowed down and stared at the colorful construction sign: NEW YOUTH CENTER OPENING NEXT MONTH. That evening, she spent two hours looking at the center's new website, clicked through every photo of the art studio, dance studio, and music room, and saved three pages of information in a folder.'

A reader makes this inference: 'Jamila is interested in the activities at the new youth center.' Which one of these is the BEST textual evidence to support that inference?
choices: Jamila took a long street instead of her usual route through the park, which shows she changed her normal behavior that day.
The construction sign said the center would open next month and displayed colorful information about the upcoming facility.
The youth center has an art studio, a dance studio, and a music room available for students to use.
She spent two hours looking at the website, clicked through every photo of the studios, and saved three pages of information.
hints: Look for the evidence that shows Jamila's own behavior and choices, not just facts about the building itself.
The strongest evidence shows what Jamila did with her time and attention, not just what exists at the center.

problemText: Read this passage about a character's response. 'When Jackson's ball rolled into the storm drain, he stared at the drain for a moment, then turned around and walked back to his house without saying anything.' Which of the following correctly describes what Jackson did in response to losing his ball?
choices: He stared at the drain, then walked back to his house without speaking.
He felt sad about losing his favorite toy and wanted to get another one from the store.
He was the kind of person who gave up easily and never faced problems directly.
He decided he would never play outside again because the drain was too dangerous.
hints: A response is what a character does, says, or thinks right after an event — look for actual actions or words in the text.
Do not pick an answer that claims a feeling or trait without showing what the character actually did.

problemText: Read the passage below. 'Chen had been avoiding his older sister all week after she borrowed his favorite comic book without asking. When she knocked on his bedroom door during dinner, Chen did not answer. After a few seconds, she left. That night, Chen quietly left the comic book on her desk before she got home from work.' What is the event that provokes Chen's response of leaving the comic book on her sister's desk?
choices: Chen's sister borrowed his favorite comic book without asking.
Chen's sister knocked on his bedroom door during dinner.
Chen avoided his older sister all week.
Chen's sister came home from work that night.
hints: The event that provokes a response comes right before the character acts. What happened immediately before Chen left the comic book on her desk?
A response must be connected to a specific moment in the story — the event that caused it.

problemText: A story says 'Aisha was brave when she entered the dark basement to find her lost cat.' Later, the text shows Aisha climbing slowly down the stairs, stopping to look around each corner before moving forward, and calling softly for the cat instead of yelling. Which statement best describes what the text actually shows versus what it claims?
choices: The text shows she is brave because it uses the word 'brave' to describe her.
The text proves she is brave by telling us she went into the dark basement.
The text claims she is brave but shows her moving carefully and calling softly.
The text claims she has a cat and shows her finding it in the basement.
hints: A claimed trait is a label the text uses in words; evidence is what the character actually does. The word 'brave' is a claim — what actions follow it?
Trust what you read about the character's actual steps and words over any single label the text assigns.

problemText: Read the two passages below that show the same character at different points in a story. At the beginning: 'Diego refused to try the new rock-climbing wall at the gym, saying he might fall and look foolish in front of the other members.' Later in the story: 'After his friend Rosa climbed the wall easily and cheered for Diego from the ground, Diego took off his shoes, gripped the first handhold, and climbed halfway up before sliding back down. When he reached the bottom, he grinned and said, "Again!" to Rosa.' Based on these two moments, which statement correctly describes how Diego changes?
choices: Diego changes because the rock-climbing wall becomes easier and safer after his first attempt at it.
Diego changes because Rosa climbs the wall successfully and Diego decides to be brave like her.
Diego changes from refusing to try climbing because he might fall to having made it halfway up the wall.
Diego changes from someone afraid to try climbing because he might fall to someone willing to attempt it despite the risk.
hints: A change compares the same kind of thing the character does at two different moments — not just describing one event as the change itself.
Look at what Diego says or does about climbing in the first moment and the last moment. What is different about his choice?

problemText: In a story, a character named Omar responds to a dropped glass by cleaning it up quickly, and the text states 'Omar was responsible.' Later, when Omar's homework assignment gets wet and ruins, he throws the ruined pages in the trash and does not redo the work before the deadline. Can you point to an event that proves Omar is responsible, based on what the text shows him doing across the whole story?
choices: No, because a claimed trait needs to be shown by the character's actions throughout the story, and his response to the ruined homework contradicts the label 'responsible.'
Yes, because Omar cleans up the dropped glass without being asked, which proves he has the character trait of responsibility in his daily life and habits.
Yes, because although Omar does not redo his homework, he still demonstrates responsibility by cleaning up the broken glass, and one good action counts as character evidence.
No, because Omar's failure to redo the homework assignment is a much larger problem than cleaning up a glass, so the small action does not prove he is truly responsible.
hints: A claimed trait is only evidence if the character's actions throughout the story match it. What does Omar actually do when faced with each problem?
Look at both moments: the dropped glass and the ruined homework. Do both actions show the same kind of behavior, or does one contradict the other?

problemText: Read the passage: 'In the first week of spring training, pitcher Marcus threw fast balls but refused to try throwing a curve ball, telling his coach, "Curve balls always go wild." During a game in mid-season, Marcus's fastball was not working, so his coach asked him to throw a curve ball. Marcus was sweating as he wound up for the pitch, but he threw it. The batter hit it into left field for an out. After the game, Marcus stayed late to practice curve balls with the coach, and by the final playoff game, Marcus threw three strikes using only curve balls and walked off the field saying "I can do both."' Based on the text, explain why "Marcus is talented" is a claimed trait and not evidence of how he changes, and identify what the text actually shows about his change.
choices: "Marcus is talented" is a claimed trait because it is a label for a character quality; his real change is that he learned to pitch during the season.
"Marcus is talented" is a claim because the text never uses that word; his real change is from refusing to throw curve balls to choosing to practice them and throwing them successfully in games.
"Marcus is talented" is a claimed trait because talent is not shown through actions; his real change is that he stopped throwing fastballs and only threw curve balls.
"Marcus is talented" is a claimed trait because the text does not say he is talented; his real change is that he got better at throwing and felt more confident about pitching.
hints: A claimed trait is a quality named in words without proof from actions. Compare what Marcus does at the start (refuses to try curve balls) to what he does at the end (practices and throws only curve balls successfully). That difference is the change.
The correct answer must name both the start moment and the end moment from the text, not just a general improvement or a single event.

problemText:
A setup is a detail placed early in a text that a later moment depends on. A payoff is the later moment where that setup actually matters. Which pair shows a setup and its payoff?

Story: Sentence 1: 'Marcus always kept his skateboard in the garage, locked to a hook so his younger cousin couldn't borrow it without asking.' Sentence 2: 'One afternoon, Marcus's cousin grabbed the skateboard anyway and rode it down the driveway.' Sentence 3: 'The skateboard was missing from the garage the next morning, and Marcus realized his cousin must have left it at the skate park.'
choices: Sentence 2 is the setup (the cousin rides it), and Sentence 3 is the payoff (it is missing).
Sentence 1 is the setup (the locked skateboard), and Sentence 3 is the payoff (the skateboard goes missing).
Sentence 1 is the setup (the garage location), and Sentence 2 is the payoff (the cousin borrows it).
Sentence 3 is the setup (the missing skateboard), and Sentence 1 is the payoff (it was locked).
hints: The setup happens first and introduces a detail; the payoff comes later when that detail matters.
Look for which sentence establishes a fact about the skateboard, then find where that fact makes a difference to the ending.

problemText:
Read this short story carefully from beginning to end, then answer the question that follows.

Sentence 1: 'Elena had a habit of writing every phone number she heard into the margins of whatever paper was nearby—a grocery list, a library receipt, even the back of a bus ticket.'
Sentence 2: 'One Tuesday, her friend Jada called and gave her the number for a pottery studio that was offering free classes for one week only.'
Sentence 3: 'Elena jotted the number down on the edge of an old envelope and stuck it in her backpack without looking at it again.'
Sentence 4: 'Three days later, Elena found the envelope while cleaning out her backpack and called the studio to sign up for the last two classes of the week.'

Which sentence is a setup that Sentence 4 depends on?
choices: Sentence 3, because Elena writes the pottery studio number down on the envelope in that sentence and saves it in her backpack where she will find it later.
Sentence 2, because it introduces the pottery studio and explains that the classes are free and only last one week, giving Elena a reason to want the number.
Sentence 1, because it shows Elena's habit of writing down numbers, which is why she has the pottery studio's number when she needs it later.
Sentence 4, because that is when Elena actually calls the studio to sign up for classes and completes the action that the story has been building toward.
hints: Ask yourself: what would stop making sense in Sentence 4 if Sentence 1 were cut out?
The setup is not the sentence that merely restates what happens in that moment; it is the earlier detail that explains why the later moment works.

problemText:
A student was asked to explain how a sentence fits into a story's overall structure and gave this answer: 'This sentence is in the middle of the story.' Explain what is wrong with this answer, then identify which of the following would be a correct answer instead.

Story detail: Sentence 1 sets up that a dog has learned to open the fence gate. Sentence 2 shows the dog escaping through the open gate. Sentence 3 describes the dog getting lost and the family searching for it.
choices: The student forgot to name which character the sentence is about and what role that character plays. A correct answer would be: This sentence is about a dog who learns to open the gate without help.
The student should have counted all the sentences in order to locate the middle one. A correct answer would be: There are three sentences total, so the middle position is Sentence 2.

The student did not explain whether the sentence belonged at the start, middle, or end of the story. A correct answer would be: This sentence is at the beginning of the story and introduces the problem.
The student only named where the sentence sits, not what it does. A correct answer would be: Sentence 1 sets up the escaped dog that Sentences 2 and 3 depend on.
hints: Naming where a part sits (beginning, middle, end) is location, not job. What does a job actually name?
A job should point to a later moment that depends on the setup—look for an answer that connects Sentence 1 to what happens after it.

problemText:
Read this story and then answer the question.

Sentence 1: 'Kenji's art class was assigned a project to paint a picture of something from their own lives, and Kenji painted the wooden pier where his grandfather used to take him fishing every summer before the family moved away.'
Sentence 2: 'A week later, Kenji's grandmother visited, and while looking at the painting hanging in his room, she asked Kenji why he had chosen such a sad subject.'
Sentence 3: 'Kenji told her it was not sad to him; it was the best place he had ever been, and he painted it to remember those mornings with his grandfather.'
Sentence 4: 'His grandmother smiled and said she had brought her old fishing tackle box from his grandfather's attic, and she handed it to Kenji.'

Sentence 1 serves more than one job in this story. Which two jobs does it do? (Select the pair that both require Sentence 1 to work.)
choices: It sets up the fishing pier as the painting's subject and establishes that detail about the setting so Sentence 2's misunderstanding and Sentence 3's explanation make sense.
It establishes that Kenji loves his grandfather and creates the painting that leads to his grandmother's visit and her decision to give him the fishing tackle box.
It explains why Kenji's family moved away from the pier and reveals that Kenji has sad feelings about it, which his grandmother notices in Sentence 2.
It sets up the painting subject and tells the entire story's plot from the very beginning in one sentence.
hints: Both jobs of Sentence 1 should point to different later moments where Sentence 1 actually pays off. Look for an answer that names two separate payoffs.
One job involves what is painted; the other involves a feeling about what is painted. Both of those details matter to why Sentence 2 and Sentence 3 happen as they do.

problemText:
A student was given this story and asked to find a setup and name its payoff.

Sentence 1: 'Every afternoon, Maya's neighbor Mr. Chen watered his plant collection in the front garden, starting with the ferns and ending with the roses, same order every day.'
Sentence 2: 'One Saturday morning, a water main broke on their street, and the water was shut off until Monday.'
Sentence 3: 'Mr. Chen carried buckets of water he had saved in his basement to keep all of his plants alive over the weekend.'
Sentence 4: 'On Monday when the water came back on, every plant in the garden was still green and healthy.'

The student answered: 'Sentence 2 is the setup because the water main breaks, and Sentence 4 is the payoff because the plants stay healthy.' Is the student correct? Why or why not?
choices: No. Sentence 1 is the setup because it shows Mr. Chen has a routine of watering daily and implicitly that he has water available for this routine, and Sentence 3 is the payoff because he uses the water he already saved.

No. Sentence 2 is not the setup; Sentence 1 is. The setup is that Mr. Chen already has saved water in his basement (established by his daily watering routine), and Sentence 3 is the payoff because he uses that water.
Yes. The student correctly identified that Sentence 2 creates the immediate problem that needs solving and Sentence 4 shows the successful result of Mr. Chen's solution with the saved water.
Yes. Sentence 2 creates the problem that forces Mr. Chen to act, and Sentence 4 demonstrates the outcome that proves the plants survived the water shortage.
hints: A true setup plants a detail that lets a later moment happen without seeming like luck or coincidence. What detail does Sentence 3 already assume exists before it happens?
Sentence 2 creates a problem, but it does not explain how Mr. Chen solves it. What earlier detail makes Sentence 3 possible?

problemText:
Read this story, paying close attention to what a setup must do to be a real structural job.

Sentence 1: 'The book sale at the library happened every spring, and this year Iris decided to volunteer at the donation table instead of just browsing.'
Sentence 2: 'While sorting books, Iris found a worn copy of a novel called 'The Starkeeper' with handwritten notes in the margins on almost every page.'
Sentence 3: 'She was so curious about the reader's notes that she bought the book instead of putting it back on the shelf.'
Sentence 4: 'Over the next month, Iris read the book slowly, reading each passage and then the note someone else had written about it, and she felt like she was having a conversation with a stranger across time.'
Sentence 5: 'When she finished, Iris wrote her own notes in a fresh copy of the same book and donated it back to the library the next spring.'

Which sentence is a setup whose payoff appears in a different sentence? Explain why it is a setup and identify the specific later moment it makes possible or meaningful.
choices: Sentence 3 is the setup. It shows Iris deciding to buy the book with notes in it, and Sentence 5 is the payoff because that is when Iris writes her own notes in a fresh copy and donates it back to the library.

Sentence 1 is the setup. It establishes that Iris volunteers at the book sale instead of just browsing like she normally does, and Sentence 2 is the payoff because that is when her volunteer job allows her to discover the marked-up book.

Sentence 2 is the setup. It introduces the book with handwritten notes, and Sentence 4 is the payoff because without the notes, Iris would not have the experience of feeling like she was having a conversation with a stranger across time.

Sentence 4 is the setup. It shows Iris reading and responding deeply to the notes in the book, which changes her understanding of reading, and Sentence 5 is the payoff because that experience motivates her to write her own notes in response.
hints: A setup plants a detail early; the payoff is where that setup actually matters to the story's meaning. Do not confuse cause-and-effect in the moment with structural setup-and-payoff across the whole story.
Ask: without Sentence 2, would Sentence 4 still make sense? Or does Sentence 4 depend on a specific detail from Sentence 2 to be true?

problemText: Which of the following is the main job of the exposition stage in a story's plot?
choices: Presents a series of problems that keep building tension
Describes the moment when the outcome of the conflict becomes decided
Shows what things look like after the conflict has been resolved
Introduces the characters, setting, and situation before any trouble begins
hints: The exposition happens first, before a conflict appears.
Look for the stage that sets up the ordinary situation, not the one that changes it.

problemText: Read this sentence from a story: 'Maya had always wanted to learn guitar, and today was finally her first lesson with Ms. Chen.' Which plot stage does this sentence belong to, and why?
choices: Exposition, because it introduces a character and her situation before any conflict appears
Rising action, because it describes Maya working toward her goal and facing new challenges
Climax, because learning guitar is the most important event that will happen in the story
Resolution, because Maya has overcome her doubts and is now getting what she wanted
hints: Ask yourself: has any trouble or complication appeared yet in this sentence?
The exposition sets up what is ordinary before anything goes wrong.

problemText: A student is reading this story and needs to find the climax. Which sentence should the student choose? 'Karim entered the poster contest at school with a design about climate change. The night before judging, a file corrupted and Karim lost most of his artwork. He worked through the night redrawing the poster by hand. At the assembly, the judges announced that Karim's poster won first prize, and he walked on stage to accept the award.'
choices: Karim entered the poster contest at school with a design about climate change, which started his whole journey toward competing.
At the assembly, the judges announced that Karim's poster won first prize, and he walked on stage to accept the award.
He worked through the night redrawing the poster by hand, which showed his commitment to completing his artwork despite losing the file.
The night before judging, a file corrupted and Karim lost most of his artwork, which forced him to find a solution to his problem.
hints: The climax is the turning point where the outcome finally becomes decided.
Look for the sentence where you find out what actually happens—not the struggle before it.

problemText: Read this partial story: 'Sasha promised to help her neighbor's garden grow before the county fair. Aphids began eating the plants, and Sasha sprayed them with soap. Then the heat wave made the soil dry out, and Sasha watered every morning. Finally, Sasha's careful watering and treatment worked, and on fair day the garden looked healthier than ever.' Which two sentences together make up the rising action, and how do you know?
choices: Only the sentence about the heat wave, because that is when tension reaches its highest point in the story
The sentences about watering and the county fair, because they show the final result and conclusion of Sasha's efforts
The sentences about aphids and heat wave, because they each describe one complication that makes the situation worse
The sentences about soap spray treatment and checking soil moisture, because those are the specific actions Sasha took to fix problems
hints: Rising action is a series of complications—more than one problem—that build tension.
The outcome is still uncertain through these sentences; the winner has not been decided yet.

problemText: A student sorted a plot incorrectly. The student labeled this sentence as the climax: 'The robot that Amir built started smoking during the school demonstration, and everyone in the audience gasped in fear.' But then the student labeled this sentence as the resolution: 'Amir quickly unplugged the robot, checked the circuit board, and found a loose wire he had missed.' Why is this sorting wrong? What should the correct labels be?
choices: The first sentence is the climax because it is the most stressful moment. The second sentence is the resolution because it solves the problem.
The first sentence should stay the climax. The second sentence is not part of the plot because it describes something too technical to matter.
The first sentence belongs in the exposition. The second sentence should be labeled rising action because it describes Amir's action of troubleshooting.
The first sentence is still rising action because the outcome has not yet been decided. The second sentence is the climax because that is when the outcome actually turns.
hints: The climax is not simply the most stressful or tense moment—it is the turning point where the outcome becomes decided.
Ask which sentence is where something decisive actually happens or is discovered that changes what will happen next.

problemText: Read this story and answer the question that follows. 'Juno and Marcus made a pact to climb the tallest hill in the park together. On hiking day, Marcus woke up sick with the flu and called Juno to say he could not go. Juno stood in her driveway, disappointed, knowing she had promised herself and Marcus she would reach the top. She decided to hike alone, and halfway up the trail she spotted Marcus sitting on a rock, his backpack next to him. Marcus explained that he felt terrible but terrible about breaking their pact more, so he came anyway even though he was still weak. The two of them made it to the top together, moving slowly, and both of them knew this hike would be different from any they had planned.' Which sentence or sentences make up the resolution, and how do you know?
choices: The sentences starting with 'Marcus explained' through the end, because by this point the outcome of the pact is already decided and the story shows what changed
Just the sentence about Marcus feeling terrible and coming anyway, because at that exact moment he makes the decision that directly solves their conflict about the pact.
The sentence about Juno standing in her driveway, because she makes the important decision to hike alone despite her disappointment and sadness.
Just the final sentence about reaching the top, because that is where they accomplish the goal they set for themselves at the very beginning.
hints: The resolution comes after the turning point, when the outcome is already decided and the story shows how things are now.
Which sentences show us what happened because of the climax—the moment when the uncertainty ended?
